parts.title: Multiple-choice cloze
parts.instruction: For questions 1–8, read the text below and decide which answer (A, B, C or D) best fits each gap.

segments.t: A few years ago, allotments seemed to belong to another age, a hobby for retired men in flat caps. Today the picture is very different. In many towns the waiting lists are so long that people may have to wait years before a plot
available. Those lucky enough to have one say the appeal is simple. After a long week in front of a screen, there is nothing like
your hands dirty.
Plot holders soon
on well with one another, swapping seeds, tools and advice. Yet the work is not always easy. A summer without rain can
a heavy toll on even the best-kept plot, and slugs can
short work of a row of young lettuces in a single night.
the effort involved, very few holders ever give up their plots. Some have even
up small businesses selling their surplus fruit and vegetables. For most, though, the real satisfaction comes from taking great pride
what they have grown themselves.

items.why: A plot ‘becomes available’ is the normal collocation; the other verbs do not combine with the adjective.
We say ‘get your hands dirty’.
‘Get on well with’ someone is the fixed phrasal verb.
‘Take a heavy toll on’ something is a fixed phrase meaning to damage it badly.
‘Make short work of’ means to deal with something quickly and easily.
‘Despite’ is followed by a noun phrase (‘the effort involved’); the others need a clause.
‘Set up a business’ is the standard phrasal verb.
We ‘take pride in’ something.

parts.title: Open cloze
parts.instruction: For questions 9–16, read the text below and think of the word which best fits each gap. Use only one word in each gap.

segments.t: Last year I decided that I was tired
eating ready meals every evening, so I signed up for a cooking course at my local college. I had never been
good cook, and my friends often joked that I could burn water. The first lesson was nothing like
I had expected. Hardly
the class begun when the teacher handed each of us a knife and an onion, and by the end of the evening my eyes
streaming.
Nevertheless, I kept going, and I now cook
least three times a week. What surprised me most was how relaxing it is: when I am slicing vegetables, I forget all about work. My neighbour,
is a keen cook herself, has even given me some of her favourite recipes. If you have ever thought about trying
new, I would strongly recommend a course like this.

items.prompt: Gap 9
items.why: ‘Tired of’ + -ing.

items.prompt: Gap 10
items.why: ‘Never been a good cook’: the indefinite article is needed.

items.prompt: Gap 11
items.why: ‘Nothing like what I had expected’.

items.prompt: Gap 12
items.why: ‘Hardly had … begun when …’ is the inverted past perfect.

items.prompt: Gap 13
items.why: Past continuous: ‘my eyes were streaming’.

items.prompt: Gap 14
items.why: ‘At least’ is a fixed phrase.

items.prompt: Gap 15
items.why: A non-defining relative clause about a person needs ‘who’ (not ‘that’).

items.prompt: Gap 16
items.why: ‘Trying something new’ (‘anything new’ also works after ‘ever’).

parts.title: Word formation
parts.instruction: For questions 17–24, read the text below. Use the word given in capitals in the question to form a word that fits in the gap. Write the new word.

segments.t: Working from home has become
common in recent years. Many employees say they are more
because there are fewer interruptions, while others value the
of choosing their own hours.
However, the arrangement is not
for everyone. People who live alone can feel
after several days without talking to a colleague, and managers sometimes worry about the
of new staff, who usually learn faster when they sit beside experienced people. Another problem is that the
between work and free time can slowly disappear.
Experts believe that the most
solution is a mixture of both: a few days at home and a few days in the office.

items.prompt: INCREASE
items.why: An adverb is needed to modify the adjective ‘common’.

items.prompt: PRODUCE
items.why: An adjective after ‘more’.

items.prompt: FLEXIBLE
items.why: A noun after ‘the’.

items.prompt: SUIT
items.why: An adjective after ‘not’: ‘not suitable for everyone’.

items.prompt: ISOLATE
items.why: ‘Feel isolated’: past participle used as an adjective.

items.prompt: TRAIN
items.why: A noun after ‘the’: ‘the training of new staff’.

items.prompt: SEPARATE
items.why: A noun is needed: ‘the separation between work and free time’.

items.prompt: SUCCESS
items.why: An adjective after ‘the most’.

parts.title: Key word transformation
parts.instruction: For questions 25–30, complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first sentence, using the word given. Do not change the word given. You must use between two and five words, including the word given.

items.prompt: I haven’t seen Maria for three years. | LAST | The ______ Maria was three years ago.
items.why: ‘The last time I saw Maria was three years ago’ keeps the meaning with the simple past.

items.prompt: ‘You should see a doctor,’ Ali told his brother. | ADVISED | Ali ______ a doctor.
items.why: ‘Advise someone to do something’ is reported advice.

items.prompt: He started learning Spanish ten years ago. | BEEN | He ______ Spanish for ten years.
items.why: Present perfect continuous for an action that began in the past and continues.

items.prompt: We will miss the train if we don’t hurry. | UNLESS | We will miss the train ______ hurry.
items.why: ‘Unless’ replaces ‘if … not’, so the second clause is positive.

items.prompt: A mechanic repaired Tom’s car yesterday. | HAD | Tom ______ yesterday.
items.why: Causative ‘have something done’ for a service done by someone else.

items.prompt: I’m sorry I didn’t phone you earlier. | WISH | I ______ you earlier.
items.why: ‘Wish’ + past perfect expresses regret about the past.

parts.title: Multiple choice: one long text
parts.instruction: For questions 31–36, read the article and choose the answer (A, B, C or D) which you think fits best according to the text.

texts.label: Article
texts.title: Up before the birds
paras: At half past two in the morning, the only light on the high street comes from the window of Hartley’s Bakery. Inside, Tomasz Kowalski, who took over the business eight years ago, is already shaping the first loaves of the day. He moves quickly but without hurry, the way people do when they have done the same thing thousands of times. “People assume I must hate this,” he says, without looking up from the dough. “They think nobody would choose to get up at one o’clock. But I did choose it.”

Tomasz was not born into baking. He trained as an accountant and spent ten years in an office, a job he describes as “perfectly fine, and perfectly forgettable”. The turning point came during a holiday, when he spent a week helping a friend at a village bakery in France. “I came back and could not stop thinking about it,” he says. “At my desk I could never point to anything and say I had made it. Here, by seven o’clock, there are two hundred loaves that did not exist the night before.”

The reality has not always been as romantic as that sounds. In his first year the business nearly failed, partly because he tried to copy the supermarket on the edge of town: dozens of products, all of them average. “I was frightened of saying no to customers,” he admits. In the end it was his oldest customer, a retired teacher called Mrs Adeyemi, who changed his mind. She told him that she would walk past three shops to buy one loaf she liked, but she would not cross the road for ten she did not. He cut the range to seven breads, and the shop has been busy ever since.

The hours remain the hardest part. Tomasz sleeps in two blocks, one in the early evening and another after lunch, and he rarely sees his friends at weekends. “It’s the social life that suffers, not the health,” he says. “I have learned to say it plainly: if you invite me to dinner on a Friday, I will be asleep by nine.” His partner, Lena, who works regular office hours, says they manage because they have stopped pretending the arrangement is normal. “We plan our time together the way other couples plan a holiday,” she says.

Not everyone in the town is convinced. A few shopkeepers think his prices are too high, and one local councillor complained about the noise of early deliveries. Tomasz took the complaints calmly. He now delivers by bicycle before four o’clock, “which seems to have satisfied everyone except the foxes”. What matters to him is that the bakery, on a high street where five shops have closed in two years, is full by eight every morning.

Asked whether he would ever go back to an office, he laughs. “I might one day, but only if somebody can show me a desk where I can smell bread at five in the morning.” He pauses, then adds more seriously: “I think the work I do is small, but it is honest. Not many people can say that about their jobs, and I never could.”

items.question: What impression does the writer give of Tomasz in the first paragraph?
options: He is worried about starting so early.
He works calmly, with the ease of long practice.
He is irritated by what people say about him.
He is rushing to finish before morning.
items.why: ‘Quickly but without hurry, the way people do when they have done the same thing thousands of times’.

items.question: What made Tomasz decide to change his career?
options: He disliked the people he worked with.
He had lost his job as an accountant.
A week working in a bakery showed him what he was missing.
A friend offered him a bakery in France.
items.why: After helping at the French bakery he ‘could not stop thinking about it’ and wanted to make something he could point to.

items.question: What did Mrs Adeyemi’s comment make Tomasz realise?
options: His shop was too far from the town centre.
Customers would pay more for fresh bread.
He should copy the supermarket more closely.
Customers value a few good products more than a large choice.
items.why: She would walk past three shops for one loaf she liked but not cross the road for ten she did not; he then cut his range to seven breads.

items.question: What does Lena’s comparison with a holiday suggest about their relationship?
options: They have to organise their time together carefully.
They go away together very often.
They find their different working hours amusing.
They argue about how to spend free time.
items.why: Couples plan a holiday deliberately; Lena says they plan time together in the same way because their schedules differ.

items.question: What does the writer say about Tomasz’s response to the complaints?
options: He ignored them because the bakery is popular.
He changed the way he makes his deliveries.
He lowered his prices for local shopkeepers.
He moved the baking to another part of town.
items.why: He now delivers by bicycle before four o’clock.

items.question: How does Tomasz feel about his work, according to the last paragraph?
options: He is unsure whether he made the right choice.
He regrets not staying in accountancy.
He sees it as modest but worthwhile.
He hopes to run a much larger business.
items.why: He calls the work ‘small, but … honest’, something he could not say about his old job.

parts.title: Gapped text
parts.instruction: For questions 37–42, you are going to read an article about a village pub. Six sentences have been removed from the article. Choose from the sentences A–G the one which fits each gap. There is one extra sentence which you do not need to use.
parts.textTitle: The pub that belongs to the village

bank.a: Shareholders do not expect to get rich from their investment.
bank.b: In the end, the target was reached with three days to spare.
bank.c: It had stood on the green for over three hundred years and was the only place in the village where people could meet.
bank.d: The committee decided to ask the community itself rather than a bank.
bank.e: He had read about a village in Devon that had bought its own shop and wondered whether a pub could work in the same way.
bank.f: The brewery has since sold several of its other pubs to a property company.
bank.g: Local builders, plumbers and electricians gave up their weekends to do much of the work for free.

segments.t: When the Red Lion in the Yorkshire village of Marsden Cross closed in 2019, residents assumed it was the end of an era.
So when a notice appeared in the post office window inviting everyone to a meeting, nearly a third of the village turned up.
The idea came from a retired engineer called Hassan Ali.
Within a week, a committee of eight volunteers had been formed.
The first problem was money. The brewery wanted £340,000 and would wait only until the end of March.
Each household was invited to buy shares at £100 each, and nobody was allowed to hold more than twenty, so that no single person could take control.
Over the following weeks, 412 people bought shares, from teenagers with their first wages to pensioners who had drunk in the pub for fifty years.
The sale went through in April.
Reopening was not easy either. The building needed a new roof, a new kitchen and a great deal of paint.
On the opening night in June, the queue stretched across the green.
Today the Red Lion is busier than it has been for years.
Instead, any profit goes into a fund for the village hall and the bus service. Hassan, who still helps behind the bar on Fridays, says the real return is simply having somewhere to go.

items.why: ‘It’ refers to the Red Lion and explains why its closing felt like the end of an era.
‘He’ is Hassan Ali, and the sentence explains where the idea came from.
It answers the money problem, and the next sentence describes how the community was asked to buy shares.
It links the 412 shareholders to the March deadline, before the sale in April.
It tells how the work listed in the previous sentence was done, before the opening night.
The following ‘Instead, any profit goes into a fund …’ contrasts with not expecting to get rich.

parts.title: Multiple matching
parts.instruction: For questions 43–52, choose from the people (A–E). The people may be chosen more than once. Five readers describe learning a musical instrument as an adult. Which person …

a.title: A · Nadia, piano
a.body: I started piano at 41, after my daughter left for university and the house suddenly felt very quiet. I found a teacher who is younger than I am, which was odd at first, but she is endlessly patient. I practise for twenty minutes before work, and I have learned that little and often works better than a long session once a week. What I did not expect was how much the lessons would calm me down: after a difficult day, ten minutes of scales does more for me than a holiday could. I still avoid playing when anyone else is in the house, though.

b.title: B · Giorgos, guitar
b.body: I bought my guitar on impulse and then left it under the bed for a year. In the end it was a video that got me going. I followed a free online course and within a month I could play three songs. The problem is that nobody tells you how much your fingers hurt at the start, and I nearly gave up in week two. Now I play in a small band with colleagues, and we perform at the staff party every December, which gives me a reason to keep improving.

c.title: C · Mei, violin
c.body: I played the violin as a child and gave it up at fifteen, so for me this is a return rather than a beginning. Everyone told me it would come back quickly. It did not. My ear was fine, but my hands had forgotten everything. I now have lessons online with a teacher in another country, and I find it easier to concentrate without anyone else in the room. The best moment so far was when my mother, who once paid for my lessons, heard me play a whole piece and cried.

d.title: D · Rob, drums
d.body: Drumming is not a quiet hobby, which was a problem in a flat with thin walls. I solved it by renting a small room at a music centre two evenings a week. People assume you need natural rhythm, but my teacher says it is mostly counting, and she is right. I am the oldest in my group by about thirty years, and the others have been wonderfully kind about it. The physical side surprised me: after an hour I am more tired than after a run.

e.title: E · Fatima, singing
e.body: I always said I could not sing, because a teacher told me so when I was nine. It took me thirty years to question that. I joined a community choir last year, mainly for company, and discovered that standing between other voices makes it much easier to find your own. We have a concert next month and I am terrified, but I would not miss it. If I could tell my younger self one thing, it would be not to let one comment decide something that big.

items.prompt: found that practising for short periods regularly is better than occasional long sessions
had to find a way of dealing with the noise made by the instrument
found the first weeks of learning physically painful
gave up the idea of singing for years because of something a teacher said
feels calmer after playing
found learning harder than other people had led them to expect
is much older than the other people who are learning
plays together with people from work
finds it easier to concentrate when taught from a distance
is nervous about a performance that is coming soon

parts.title: Part 1 · Essay (compulsory)
parts.instruction: Question 1. You must answer this question. Write your answer in 140–190 words in an appropriate style.

tasks.title: Question 1 · Essay
tasks.situation: In your English class you have been talking about transport in cities. Now your teacher has asked you to write an essay.
tasks.prompt: Write an essay using all the notes and give reasons for your point of view. Statement: Cities should do more to encourage people to leave their cars at home. Do you agree?
tasks.model:
Many cities are now trying to persuade people to leave their cars at home. In my opinion, they are right to do so, although it has to be done carefully.
The most important step is to improve public transport. Nobody will give up a car if the bus is slow, crowded or only comes once an hour. If trains and buses are frequent, clean and reliable, many drivers will happily change their habits.
Money matters too. Fuel, parking and insurance make driving expensive, and city councils could add to this by charging cars that enter the busiest streets. On the other hand, this might be unfair to people on low incomes who have no other way of getting to work, so the money raised should be spent on cheaper tickets.
A further idea is to create safe cycle lanes, so that short journeys can be made by bike. This would also make the air cleaner.
In conclusion, cities should certainly encourage people to drive less, but they must offer a real alternative first.
checklist: Content: I gave my opinion and covered both notes plus an idea of my own.
Communicative achievement: a neutral or formal tone, with reasons for my view.
Organisation: an introduction, a paragraph for each point and a conclusion, with linking words.
Language: a range of vocabulary and structures (conditionals, modal verbs), with few mistakes.
Length: 140–190 words.

parts.title: Part 2 · Choose one task
parts.instruction: Questions 2–4. Write an answer to ONE of the questions 2–4 in this part. Write your answer in 140–190 words in an appropriate style.

tasks.title: Question 2 · Article
tasks.situation: You see this notice in an English-language magazine for local residents.
tasks.prompt: Articles wanted: The best place to relax in my town. Tell us about a place where you go to relax, why you like it and what could make it even better. We will publish the best articles. Write your article.
points: say why you like going there
tasks.model:
My place to switch off
When I need a break from work, I walk ten minutes to Riverside Park, my favourite place to relax in town. It is not large, but it has everything I need: old trees, a quiet café and a long path along the water.
I usually go on Sunday mornings, when it is still peaceful. I take a book, buy a coffee and sit on the bench by the little bridge. Watching the ducks and listening to the water helps me forget the week behind me. In summer there is sometimes live music, which makes the park feel like the heart of the community.
However, the park could be even better. At the moment there are not enough bins, and the toilets are often closed. I would also like to see more benches near the playground, so that parents can sit down while their children play.
If the council made these small changes, Riverside Park would be perfect. In the meantime, I recommend a visit to anyone who needs a few quiet hours.
checklist: Content: I described the place, gave reasons and made one suggestion.
Communicative achievement: a lively, friendly tone that suits a magazine article, with a title.
Organisation: a clear opening, paragraphs for each point and a closing sentence.
Language: descriptive vocabulary, a mix of tenses, and few mistakes.
Length: 140–190 words.

tasks.title: Question 3 · Email
tasks.situation: You have received an email from your English-speaking friend Sam, who is planning to visit you.
tasks.prompt: Sam wrote: ‘I’m planning to visit you for a long weekend in the spring! What should I pack? What would you like us to do? And is there anything I should know about getting around?’ Write your email to Sam.
points: what to pack, and the weather
how to get to your home
tasks.model:
Hi Sam,
That’s fantastic news! I can’t wait to see you. Spring is a lovely time to visit, but the weather can change quickly, so please bring a warm jumper and a waterproof jacket as well as something lighter for sunny afternoons. Comfortable shoes are a must, because I’d like to show you the old town on foot.
On Saturday we could walk up to the castle and have lunch at a market I know, where you can try some local food. If the weather is good, we might hire bikes on Sunday and cycle along the canal. Let me know if you would prefer something more relaxing.
Getting here is easy. A train runs from the airport to the central station every half hour, and the journey takes about forty minutes. Buy your ticket from the machine, as it is cheaper than buying it on the train. I will meet you at the station.
Let me know your arrival time as soon as you have booked your flight.
Best wishes,
Ana
checklist: Content: I answered all three of Sam’s questions.
Communicative achievement: a friendly, informal tone (contractions, a greeting and a sign-off).
Organisation: short paragraphs, one for each topic.
Language: suggestions (we could …, we might …), advice (please bring …) and few mistakes.
Length: 140–190 words.

tasks.title: Question 4 · Review
tasks.situation: A website for English learners is collecting reviews written by its readers.
tasks.prompt: Write a review of a film that you have seen recently. Say what the film is about, what you liked and disliked, and whether you would recommend it to other people.
tasks.model:
The Lighthouse Letters: a quiet film with a big heart
The Lighthouse Letters tells the story of Ingrid, a young woman who inherits her grandfather’s lighthouse on a remote island. While clearing his belongings, she discovers a box of letters that slowly reveals a secret from his past.
What I liked most was the photography. The island, with its grey skies and wild water, is almost a character in itself. The two main actors are also very convincing, and their scenes together are warm and funny without ever feeling forced.
On the other hand, the middle of the film is rather slow, and a few of the minor characters are not developed enough. Some viewers may find the ending too sentimental.
Overall, I would recommend the film to anyone who enjoys thoughtful stories rather than fast action. Take a friend, and bring a handkerchief.
checklist: Content: I explained the story briefly, gave likes and dislikes, and made a recommendation.
Communicative achievement: an opinion-led tone that keeps the reader interested, without giving away the ending.
Organisation: a title, a paragraph for the story, one for opinions and a final recommendation.
Language: evaluative adjectives and linking words such as ‘on the other hand’ and ‘overall’, with few mistakes.
Length: 140–190 words.

parts.title: Eight short extracts
parts.instruction: For questions 1–8, you will hear people talking in eight different situations. For each question, choose the best answer (A, B or C). You will hear each extract twice.

script.t: Hello, Mr Okafor, it’s Sandra from the Eastgate Dental Practice. I’m calling about your appointment tomorrow at ten o’clock. I’m afraid Dr Hughes has to go on a training day, so we’ll need to move you. I can offer you Thursday at half past two, or the following Monday, first thing in the morning. If neither of those suits you, please ring reception on 0117 496 0123 and we’ll find something else. Oh, and there’s no need to bring the form again, we already have it. Thank you, bye.
So, how are you finding the new gym?
Well, I thought I’d love it. The equipment’s brilliant, and it’s actually cheaper than my old one. But in the evenings it’s so busy that I spend half the time waiting for a machine.
Can’t you go at a different time?
I’m thinking of trying six in the morning. I’m not sure I’m a morning person, though.

Before we finish, just a quick reminder. From Monday, the kitchen on the second floor will be closed while it’s being refitted, so please use the one on the ground floor instead. I know, builders, noise, dust, it won’t be pretty, but it should only take three weeks. And if anyone has ideas about what we’d like in the new kitchen, put them in the box by reception before Friday.
Well done, that went really well.
Did it? I couldn’t stop thinking about the slide that wouldn’t load. I kept waiting for someone to say something.
Nobody noticed. They were too busy taking notes.
I suppose so. I just wish I’d practised the ending a bit more.

People always ask why I don’t just fly, and yes, the plane’s quicker. But on the sleeper I have dinner, go to bed, and wake up in the Highlands. No airport queues, no early start. The beds are small, I won’t pretend otherwise, and the tea is dreadful. Nor is it cheaper than a budget flight. But arriving somewhere without feeling I’ve been processed, that’s what I love.
Shall I book the Italian place for Friday? Eight o’clock?
Friday’s fine. The thing is, it’s so noisy in there, and we’ll want to talk. What about that new Lebanese place near the library? It’s bigger and much quieter.
I haven’t been. Is it expensive?
Not at all.
Okay, I’ll ring them tomorrow.

I signed up for the half marathon in a moment of madness, and everyone I know thinks I’ve lost my mind. I haven’t lost a single pound since January, if that’s what you’re wondering. But I sleep like a baby, and I’ve made friends on the Saturday group run. So whatever happens on the day, it’s been worth it.

People say high streets are dying because of the internet, and in a way that’s true. But when someone brings back a jumper they ordered online, it’s usually because it didn’t fit, and that’s where we come in. We can’t compete on price, so we compete on service. The shops that will survive are the ones where the staff know your name.

items.question: Why is Sandra calling?
items.why: Dr Hughes is away, so ‘we’ll need to move you’ to Thursday or Monday.

items.question: What problem does the man have with the gym?
options: It is too crowded in the evening.
items.why: ‘In the evenings it’s so busy that I spend half the time waiting for a machine.’

items.question: What is the speaker doing?
items.why: The second-floor kitchen will be closed for three weeks.

items.question: How does the woman feel about her presentation?
items.why: She is bothered by the slide that would not load and wishes she had practised the ending.

items.question: What does the man like most about travelling on the sleeper train?
options: He avoids the stress of airports.
items.why: He mentions no airport queues and not feeling ‘processed’; he says it is not cheaper and the beds are small.

items.question: What does the man suggest?
items.why: He says Friday is fine but proposes the Lebanese place instead of the noisy Italian one.

items.question: What does the woman say about her training?
items.why: She has not lost a pound, but she ‘sleeps like a baby’.

items.question: What does the speaker think about the future of high-street shops?
options: They will survive if they offer good service.
items.why: He says shops cannot compete on price, so they compete on service, and those will survive.

parts.title: Sentence completion
parts.instruction: For questions 9–18, you will hear a guide talking to a group of visitors at a nature reserve. For each question, write a word or short phrase in the gap. You will hear the recording twice.

script.t: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Millbrook Wetland Centre. My name’s Helen and I’ll be your guide for the next two hours. Before we set off, a few practical points. The centre covers about sixty hectares, but don’t worry, the main path is flat and only four kilometres long, so you won’t need hiking boots. Ordinary walking shoes are fine. The reserve was created in 1996 on the site of an old gravel quarry, and today it’s home to over two hundred species of birds. Our most famous residents are the otters, which were brought back to the area in 2008. You’re most likely to see them at dawn, I’m afraid, but we’ll look for signs of them on our walk this morning. Now, our route. We’ll start at the main lake, where you can see the ducks and swans, then follow the boardwalk through the reed beds. If we’re quiet, we may spot a kingfisher. It’s small and bright blue, and it usually sits on the wooden posts along the water. At the far end there’s a hide with a view over the shallow pools, and that’s where we’ll stop for a hot drink. The café there is run by volunteers, and all the profits go to conservation. Please remember not to feed the birds, because bread is actually harmful to them. And finally, if you enjoy today, you can become a member for thirty-five pounds a year, which includes free entry and a magazine. Right, if everyone’s ready, let’s go.

items.prompt: The main path in the reserve is ______ kilometres long.
items.why: ‘Only four kilometres long’.

items.prompt: Visitors do not need hiking boots because ordinary ______ are fine.
items.why: ‘Ordinary walking shoes are fine’.

items.prompt: The reserve was created on the site of an old ______.
items.why: ‘On the site of an old gravel quarry’.

items.prompt: More than ______ species of birds live in the reserve.
items.why: ‘Over two hundred species of birds’.

items.prompt: Otters were brought back to the area in ______.
items.why: ‘Brought back to the area in 2008’.

items.prompt: The best chance of seeing otters is at ______.
items.why: ‘You’re most likely to see them at dawn’.

items.prompt: Kingfishers usually sit on ______ along the water.
items.why: ‘It usually sits on the wooden posts’.

items.prompt: At the far end, the group will visit a ______ with a view over the shallow pools.
items.why: ‘At the far end there’s a hide with a view over the shallow pools’.

items.prompt: Visitors are asked not to feed the birds with ______.
items.why: ‘Bread is actually harmful to them’.

items.prompt: Membership costs £______ a year.
items.why: ‘Thirty-five pounds a year’.

parts.title: Five short monologues
parts.instruction: For questions 19–23, you will hear five different people talking about a hobby they gave up. For each speaker, choose from the list (A–H) the reason why they stopped. Use the letters only once. There are three extra letters which you do not need to use. You will hear the recordings twice.

pool.b: An injury made it too risky.
pool.c: The speaker moved to a new area.
pool.d: A new job left too little time.
pool.e: The group that organised it came to an end.
pool.f: The speaker lost confidence after a poor result.
pool.g: The speaker felt too old for it.

script.t: I played the cello in an amateur orchestra for ten years, and I loved every minute. Then my husband got a job in Aberdeen and we packed up and went north. I did look for another orchestra, but the nearest one rehearses an hour’s drive away. Nobody’s been unfriendly, and I haven’t lost interest. I still play at home most evenings. I just haven’t found the right place yet.

I played five-a-side football on Tuesday evenings with the same lads for years. Then last winter I twisted my knee quite badly. The doctor told me it could easily happen again, and I wasn’t prepared to take the risk. I do miss it, and I still go along to watch, but swimming’s my thing now.

I sang in a choir for about six years. We rehearsed in the church hall, until the church was sold last spring. We looked around for somewhere else, but there was nowhere that suited us, and after a few months of meeting in each other’s kitchens it just faded away. A shame, because the singing was never the problem. We still have a group chat.

I loved sailing, but a boat is a bottomless pit. Mooring fees, insurance, repairs, new sails. In the end I worked out I was spending more every month than I pay in rent, and that was that. I sold the boat to a young couple, and they seem to be having a lovely time.

I went to a painting class every Wednesday evening until I was promoted last year. Now I often work late, or I’m travelling, and I can’t promise to turn up every week. My teacher still emails me, which is kind of her. I would love to go back, and I hope that one day I will.

items.prompt: Speaker 1
items.why: Her husband’s job in Aberdeen meant they moved north.

items.prompt: Speaker 2
items.why: He twisted his knee and would not risk it happening again.

items.prompt: Speaker 3
items.why: The choir lost its rehearsal room and faded away.

items.prompt: Speaker 4
items.why: The boat cost more each month than his rent.

items.prompt: Speaker 5
items.why: Since her promotion she works late and travels.

parts.title: Radio interview
parts.instruction: For questions 24–30, you will hear an interview with a woman called Gina Marsh, who runs a repair café. For each question, choose the best answer (A, B or C). You will hear the recording twice.

script.t: My guest today is Gina Marsh, who started a repair café in her home town three years ago. Gina, welcome. What was the idea behind it?

Well, it wasn’t a grand plan, to be honest. My toaster broke, and the shop told me it would cost more to repair than to replace it. That made me so cross that I took it to a neighbour who fixes radios as a hobby. He mended it in ten minutes, for nothing. I thought, why isn’t everybody doing this? So I booked the village hall for one Saturday morning and put up a few posters.
And how many people came?
Forty, which was a shock. I’d have been happy with ten. We ran out of tables and chairs, and one man had to stand holding his lamp for an hour while he waited for a free volunteer.
What do people bring along?

You’d think it would be electrical things, and we get plenty of those, but what we see most is clothes. Zips, hems, jackets that have lost a button. They’re the easiest to fix, and the volunteers who sew are always the busiest. The hardest things are laptops. Often there’s nothing we can do.
Do you get disappointed when something can’t be repaired?

Less than you’d think. People are usually grateful anyway, because they’ve learned why it broke. And we always say, don’t be embarrassed to ask, because most of the time the answer is a loose wire or a blocked filter, something anyone could do with a little help.
Do younger people come?

More than I expected. I assumed it would be mostly pensioners, but students turn up with their bicycles and headphones. They often stay to help someone else, and that’s my favourite thing. A fifteen-year-old taught a woman of eighty how to replace the cord on her vacuum cleaner. They were both delighted.
Is the café a way to change how we shop?

I’d like to think it helps, but I’m realistic. People will still buy cheap things. What I hope is that when something breaks, they stop and ask, can this be mended? Even if the answer is no. If that question becomes automatic, we’ve achieved something. The money we collect in donations, by the way, pays for the tools, not for anyone’s wages. We’re all volunteers.

items.question: Why did Gina start the repair café?
options: She wanted to earn money from repairs.
A neighbour’s free repair gave her the idea.
She had trained as an electrician.
items.why: The neighbour mended her toaster for nothing, and she thought everybody should be able to get this.

items.question: How did Gina feel about the first event?
options: surprised at how many people came
disappointed by how few people came
worried that there were too few volunteers
items.why: Forty came, when she would have been happy with ten.

items.question: What do visitors bring most often?
items.why: ‘What we see most is clothes.’

items.question: What does Gina say about things that cannot be repaired?
options: Their owners are usually still glad of the help.
Their owners ask for their money back.
items.why: ‘People are usually grateful anyway.’

items.question: What does Gina like best about younger visitors?
options: They bring unusual things to repair.
items.why: ‘They often stay to help someone else, and that’s my favourite thing.’

items.question: What is Gina’s hope for the repair café?
options: that people will stop buying cheap goods
that people will think about repairing before throwing things away
that shops will sell more spare parts
items.why: She hopes people will ask ‘can this be mended?’ when something breaks.

items.question: What is the money from donations used for?
items.why: ‘Pays for the tools, not for anyone’s wages.’

parts.title: Part 1 · Interview
parts.instruction: The examiner asks each candidate some general and personal questions about everyday topics such as home, work, free time and travel. Answer in two or three full sentences, and give a reason or an example. In the exam this part takes about 2 minutes.

tasks.title: Part 1 · Interview
tasks.situation: Two candidates and an examiner. The examiner asks each of you a few questions.

card.title: Examiner’s questions
lines: Where are you from? What do you like about the place?
What do you usually do at the weekend?
Tell us about a trip you would like to take.
What kind of food do you enjoy cooking or eating?
How do you usually get to work or to your classes?

redemittel: I’m from … It’s a … town/city in …
What I like most about it is …
It depends. If the weather is good, I …; otherwise I …
I’d really love to go to … because …
I’ve always been interested in …
tasks.model:
Where are you from? I’m from a small town near the coast. I’ve lived there all my life, apart from two years when I studied in a bigger city. What I like most about it is that everything is close, and you can walk to the beach in ten minutes.
What do you usually do at the weekend? It depends. If the weather is good, I try to get outside, perhaps go for a long walk or meet friends for a picnic. If it’s raining, I’m usually at home, cooking or watching a series.
Tell us about a trip you would like to take. I’d love to go to Iceland. I’ve always wanted to see the northern lights, and I enjoy places with lots of space and very few people.
checklist: I answered with full sentences, not just one word.
I gave a reason or an example for each answer.
I spoke clearly and at a natural speed.
I used a range of tenses (present, past, ‘would like to’).

parts.title: Part 2 · Long turn
parts.instruction: The examiner gives you two photographs and asks you a question about them. Compare the photographs and answer the question. You have about 1 minute. Then your partner has about 30 seconds to comment on your photographs. In the exam you do not get any preparation time.

tasks.title: Part 2 · Two photographs
tasks.situation: Look at the two photographs described below. Compare them, and say why the people have chosen to eat in these places.

slides.title: Photo 1
lines: A family is having a picnic on a blanket in a park.
The sun is shining and two children are playing nearby.

slides.title: Photo 2
lines: Two friends are sitting at a small table in a busy café.
They are eating sandwiches and looking at a phone.

card.title: Why have the people chosen to eat in these places?
lines: Compare the two photographs and answer the question (about 1 minute).
Your partner then says, in about 30 seconds, which of the two places they would prefer.

redemittel: Both photos show …, but in the first one … whereas in the second …
One difference is that …
I suppose the family have chosen to … because …
They might be doing this because …
They look as if they are …
In the background I can see …
tasks.model:
Both photographs show people eating, but in very different places. In the first one, a family is having a picnic in a park, while in the second two friends are sitting in a busy café.
I suppose the family have chosen a picnic because it is cheap and the children can run around. It also looks like a sunny day, so it is pleasant to be outside, and they can stay as long as they like. The friends, on the other hand, might have chosen the café because they only have a short time, perhaps during their lunch break, and they want something quick and convenient. They may also want to be in the middle of the town, where it is lively.
In both cases, I think the people want to enjoy their time together. The family look relaxed and the friends look as if they are catching up on news.
checklist: I compared the photos instead of describing each one separately.
I answered the question: why have the people chosen to eat there?
I used speculation (might, may, perhaps, I suppose, they look as if …).
I kept talking for about a minute, with linking words.

parts.title: Part 3 · Collaborative task
parts.instruction: Talk to your partner about the question on the card, using the five prompts. Discuss each idea, give your opinions and react to your partner. After about 2 minutes, the examiner asks you to decide which two ideas would be best. In the exam this part takes about 3 minutes.

tasks.title: Part 3 · Attracting visitors
tasks.situation: A town council wants to attract more visitors. Talk to your partner about how each idea could help. Then decide which two ideas would be the most effective.

card.title: How could the town attract more visitors?
lines: a food festival
better train and bus links
a new museum
cheaper hotels
a weekly market

redemittel: Shall we start with …?
What do you think about …?
I’m not sure that would work, because …
That’s a good point, but …
I see what you mean, however …
So, which two shall we choose?
I think we both agree that … and … would be the best.
tasks.model:
A: Shall we start with the food festival? I think it could bring a lot of people, because everyone likes food.
B: That’s a good point, but it would only happen once a year. A weekly market would bring people more regularly, and they could buy local products.
A: I see what you mean. And what about better transport? If it’s hard to reach the town, people won’t come, however good the attractions are.
B: Absolutely. I’m not sure a new museum would work, though. It would cost a lot, and many towns already have one.
A: Cheaper hotels might help families, but I’m not sure that is the main reason people visit.
B: So, which two shall we choose?
A: I think transport and the weekly market would be the most effective.
B: I agree. Let’s go for those.
checklist: I discussed all five prompts, not just one or two.
I invited my partner’s opinion and reacted to it.
I gave reasons for my views.
We reached a decision together at the end.

parts.title: Part 4 · Discussion
parts.instruction: The examiner asks you and your partner further questions connected with the topic of Part 3. Give your own opinions, answer your partner’s comments and explain your reasons. In the exam this part takes about 4 minutes.

tasks.title: Part 4 · Tourism and travel
tasks.situation: Discuss these questions with your partner. The examiner may ask each of you a different question.

card.title: Examiner’s questions
lines: Do you think tourism is always good for a town? Why (not)?
What can visitors do to respect the places they visit?
Do you prefer to travel to quiet places or to busy cities?
Is it better to travel often for short trips, or rarely for a long time?
How important is it for a town to keep its traditions?

redemittel: In my opinion, … because …
I tend to think that …
On the one hand …, but on the other hand …
That’s true, although …
I’d say it depends on …
What about you? Do you agree?
tasks.model:
Do you think tourism is always good for a town? I’d say it depends. On the one hand, tourists bring money and jobs, especially to small places. On the other hand, too many visitors can push up prices and make life harder for local people, for example by making housing more expensive.
What can visitors do to respect the places they visit? I think the most important thing is to be considerate. They can avoid dropping litter, keep the noise down in residential areas, and shop in local businesses instead of big chains.
Do you prefer quiet places or busy cities? I tend to prefer quiet places, because I like to relax on holiday. But I agree with you that cities can be exciting for a weekend, and you can see a lot in a short time.
checklist: I gave my own opinion and a reason, not just ‘yes’ or ‘no’.
I responded to what my partner said.
I used a range of vocabulary connected with travel and towns.
I did not interrupt my partner and I took my turn.
